articles.title: China tightens travel restrictions for citizens
articles.summary: Observers say the new rules will further tighten the Chinese government's control over its citizens.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Chinese citizens could now be banned from leaving China for up to three years for criminal activities that endanger national security By Abel U ,  BBC Chinese   and   Koh Ewe 
- Published 15 September 2026 
China has imposed a range of sweeping new rules restricting travel in and out of the country in a move that observers say will give the government even more control over its citizens. 
Citizens deemed to have "harmed" China's national security or interests while overseas can also be barred from leaving China for up to three years. 
But the law also says that it will apply to anyone considered a threat to the country's industrial or technological security. 
China keeps close scrutiny on sectors like semiconductors and AI, as the race between Beijing and Washington for tech dominance heats up. According to reports, travel restrictions were earlier imposed on some executives from these industries. 
In March, the co-founders of Manus - an AI company that had been acquired by Meta - were reportedly barred from leaving China. 
Under the new rules, border officials are now also required to advise Chinese nationals against travelling to countries and regions deemed "high-risk". 
But even prior to the rules being announced, some people were already restricted from going to certain countries. Civil servants were among the earliest groups subjected to these controls, which later expanded to include state-owned enterprise employees and ordinary citizens. 
A retired grassroots civil servant in Anhui told BBC Chinese that around 2018, his workplace made employees surrender their passports. His passport remains in the custody of his former employer even though he retired last year. 
According to the ex-civil servant, employees had to apply and explain their reasons for overseas travel, and not all requests were approved. 
For example, trips to visit relatives were more likely to be approved than tourism trips, he said. 
"It is mainly to prevent corrupt officials from fleeing or transferring assets abroad," he said. "For more senior officials, it may also be intended to prevent the disclosure of state secrets." 
A man identified by his pseudonym, Xiao Wang, who works at a state-owned financial institution in Beijing, told BBC Chinese that his fellow employees have long been required to surrender their passports and get approval for overseas travel. 
The 32-year-old said managers have verbally reminded staff that "sensitive countries such as Japan are definitely off-limits". 
Professor Tom Kellogg, Executive Director of the Center for Asian Law at Georgetown University, told BBC Chinese that the expanding travel restrictions were "deeply concerning" and said they reflect a "growing ideological control under Chinese leader Xi Jinping", which is reminiscent of Mao Zedong's era. 
China was largely cut off from the world under Mao's decades-long regime, and international travel only became a part of life for Chinese people in the 1990s, after China underwent a series of reforms and opening up. 
Today's various travel restrictions, Kellogg said, "bring back memories of that painful era". 
Image source, VCG via Getty Images Image caption, 
Some in China, including civil servants and employees at state-owned enterprises, face travel restrictions 
Piyao, a Chinese government "rumour-refuting" platform, posted a statement last week saying the new rules "do not restrict the travel of ordinary citizens, but rather serve as a preventative measure against high-risk destinations and individuals with unusual travel patterns". 
The regulations were issued to address "problems" such as people being deceived into leaving the country or engaging in illegal gambling and scam activities abroad, the statement said. 
According to publicly available information, Chinese citizens currently cannot check whether they are subject to exit controls on their own. 
Unless official written or verbal notification is issued, people generally only discover they are restricted from leaving when applying for documents or attempting to depart. 
China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and immigration authorities did not respond to enquiries from BBC Chinese. 
Chinese authorities have drastically stepped up exit bans on its citizens in recent years, according to data provided to the BBC from rights group Safeguard Defenders. 
China's supreme court database showed only 89 records mentioning exit bans in 2016, but that figure had risen to 188,760 last year. 
The percentage of civil verdicts that dealt with exit bans also surged more than 30 times between 2019 and 2025, from around 0.23% to 7.3%. The actual volume of such cases is believed to be even higher, owing to an increasing number of withheld judgments. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Pipi said he was questioned by state security police after attending 2019 protests in Hong Kong 
The rules could also affect citizens who work in areas such as human rights, say analysts. 
"This is another tool designed to control what Chinese citizens do and say overseas," said Professor Kellogg. 
"In some cases, in order to prevent individuals from criticising the Chinese government overseas or to punish their rights advocacy activities, state security authorities directly refuse to issue passports." 
One 26-year-old Chinese citizen, who wished to be identified only as Pipi, told BBC Chinese that his passport application in 2023 was rejected and he believes it was because he attended the massive pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong in 2019. 
According to Pipi, he was interviewed by Hong Kong media outlets during the protests. When he returned to mainland China, he was questioned by state security police. 
He said one immigration official told him that he could not get a passport "because of the Hong Kong issue" – but this was not confirmed in writing to him. 
"I don't know whether I'll ever be able to leave [China]," he said.

articles.title: China criticises idea it is in 'malicious competition' over AI
articles.summary: It follows the Anthropic CEO's calls for a slowdown in AI development - but in a way that prevents China from pulling ahead in the race.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Xi Jinping at the World AI Conference, which was held in China in July By Koh Ewe 
- Published 14 September 2026 
China has hit out against what it has called "threat narratives" over AI governance and warned against "engaging in confrontation and malicious competition". 
It follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development - but in a way that prevents China from pulling ahead in the AI race. 
Over the past week, industry insiders at the leading US artificial intelligence labs have been warning in extremely stark terms about the potential threat AI poses, with some saying it could wipe out humanity. 
But US President Donald Trump has said that his priority is making sure the US develops the tech faster than China. 
- 
Tech stocks fall after calls for AI development to slow down 
- 
Questions mount over what an AI 'slowdown' would look like 
- Published 3 days ago 
- 
Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans' 
- Published 9 September 
On Monday, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters that "narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance and are not in anyone's interest". 
"All parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good," he added. 
His comments highlight the difficulties in getting an agreement between the world's two leading AI powers. 
An agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is "next to impossible", says Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor with the military studies programme at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies. 
"As part of each state's core national security interests, cooperation in taking things slower and more safely in relation to AI, is very, very unlikely." 
Artificial intelligence now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech. Despite US export bans on critical chips, Chinese AI innovation has been expanding, driven by open-source technology and Beijing's backing. 
Many experts believe the US is still ahead, and Chinese firms are trying to catch up as they struggle to raise the hundreds of billions of dollars that investors are ploughing into American AI. 
But Beijing, including Chinese leader Xi Jinping himself, has also spoken about the risks posed by AI. China must "balance development and security", and introduce and improve relevant laws and ethical guidelines, and strengthen prevention of risks, to "safeguard the interests of the people and national security", state security minister Chen Yixin wrote on Sunday. 
He warned of the dangers of "hostile forces" such as foreign intelligence using AI and called for international cooperation. 
"There are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks," Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote recently. 
China has "technical reasons" to work with the US, she argues, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China, and detect and understand vulnerabilities. 
In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation, which aims to shape global AI governance. And speaking at the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Xi proposed creating a community for open-source AI. 
All this comes as calls for AI regulation grow louder in the US, especially after a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week that "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued. 
Since then top industry bosses, such as Dario Amodei, have called for a slowdown and more regulation. 
"We need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities," Open AI's chief executive Sam Altman wrote on X on Monday, which was echoed by Microsoft boss Satya Nadella who said AI development "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities". 
But US President Donald Trump downplayed the risks , saying that he wanted to keep the US's lead over China "because whoever wins AI, wins". 
The competition is fierce. 
The former Anthropic employee Coxon told the BBC that there needed to be " some sort of coordinated slowdown with China , if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale". 
As Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week, the two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, the South China Morning Post reports. 
It is also likely to be part of the talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, who are trying to meet before next week's summit, the paper said. Vice-Premier He runs the agency that oversees the country's economic planning, including AI development. 
While collaboration between the US and China is important, experts say the stakes are high for both countries. 
"If China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, this will not be viewed in Washington as losing a technology race," says Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based firm, Forani Investments. 
"It will be viewed as losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era."

articles.title: Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine
articles.summary: North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so, writes the BBC's Quentin Sommerville.
articles.full_text:
By Quentin Sommerville International Correspondent, Seoul 
An enemy that swarmed the battlefield in large groups while under fire, seemingly oblivious to the dangers of drones and fire from automatic weapons. An elite corps of ghost soldiers who chose suicide over surrender. They fought and died in their thousands, then apparently vanished from the battlefield. 
North Korea's soldiers were sent to fight by Pyongyang alongside Russian forces as they sought to repel a Ukrainian offensive on Moscow's territory at the end of 2024. They paid a heavy price, as many as 3,000 killed in action from the 13,000 deployed. 
Ultimately, they would adapt their tactics, and with Russia would drive Ukrainian forces from its Kursk region. In combat terms, little has been heard of them since, but according to Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, North Korean forces, and their weaponry, are soon to make a dramatic return to Russia's war in Ukraine. 
Last month, Zelensky warned that up to 50,000 North Koreans will be deployed in Russia, revising an earlier estimate of 30,000 troops. He called on South Korea to provide support for his country's air defence. 
But why, after such heavy losses, would North Korea send more men to fight for Russia, and what happened to its soldiers sent in the first place? 
"They're still there", said Dr Yang Uk, research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Center for Foreign Policy and National Security in Seoul. "They are defending Russian territory for another counterattack from Ukraine. And we believe that some of the engineer corps or workers might be in [the Russian-occupied] Donbas area but that's not the combat troops." 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Zelensky has warned that as many as 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed in Russia 
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, HUR, estimates that 8,500 North Korean servicemen are still on Russian territory. They are organised into four brigades, which operate as part of the "North" Group of Forces and are assigned to protecting the state border of the Russian Federation in the Kursk Region from Ukrainian incursions. 
"They do not participate in active combat operations. Units of the Korean People's Army have not been observed in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," HUR said in a statement to the BBC. 
A first for North Korea 
For North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, the Kursk deployment was a gamble, its largest combat force ever sent overseas. (In 1973, North Korea sent 1,500 military personnel and instructors to Egypt during the Yom Kippur war with Israel, and in the late 1960s, an estimated 87 North Korean pilots fought for the North Vietnamese against US forces). 
And despite the bloodshed, it was a gamble that paid off, reaping countless benefits for the isolated and impoverished country, transforming both its economic and military fortunes. And one that could serve as a blueprint for even deeper military cooperation. 
North Koreans, "now know what modern combat is about", said Yang. 
The soldiers sent to fight in Russia were from Storm Corps, the elite of the North Korean armed forces. Extremely isolated, totalitarian North Korea is a militarised and heavily indoctrinated state. 
At first, neither Russia, nor North Korea, even acknowledged their presence. Ukrainian forces first clashed with them in November 2024, and the first live North Korean prisoners of war wouldn't be captured until January of the following year. 
It wasn't until April 2025 that Russia first acknowledged their role, when Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, described their "heroism" on the battlefield. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
For Kim Jong Un, sending North Korean troops to Kursk was a gamble. It was the largest combat force North Korea had ever sent overseas 
Yang continued, "North Korean soldiers are very brave I mean, especially those of Storm Corps. They are willing to die for their country. But the problem is that passion doesn't mean efficient combat skills... [They suffered] a lot of bloodshed in the early stage of the Kursk campaign, but they learned the lessons of modern drone warfare." 
"Cannon fodder", is how "Sultan", a soldier with Ukraine's 95th Air Assault Brigade described North Korean troops. He faced them in the battle for Kursk at the end of 2024. 
"They would begin with one large assault group, then another 15–20 men would be sent into the same position, and then more after that. The North Koreans operated differently. They kept moving all the time. That gave them a certain advantage, but not a decisive one," he recalled recently in Kyiv. 
Communication between them and their Russian allies appeared poor, he said, and their soldiers were inadequately equipped. 
After combat, Sultan and his men would search enemy corpses for documents and intelligence information. On the Russian dead they would find personal belongings, identification and equipment. "But when we searched the North Koreans specifically, the only thing we found on them was simply ammo. We checked absolutely all the small pockets - there were no documents, nothing at all," he explained. 
Other Ukrainian soldiers reported the North Koreans lacked body armour, winter clothing and helmets. 
In one chilling video from a Ukrainian assault, a wounded North Korean soldier lies prone on the snow-covered ground in a wooded area. As the Ukrainians approach, he detonates a grenade under his chin, after calling out, with his last words, the name of his leader, Kim Jong Un. 
In April 2025, at a memorial service in Pyongyang at the newly created Museum of Foreign Military Operations, Kim praised heroes who choose suicide over capture. 
In a speech to relatives, with Russia's Defence Minister Andrey Belousov in attendance, he said they were "heroes who unhesitatingly opted for self-blasting, suicide attack, in order to defend the great honour". 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Speaking to relatives of the soldiers, with Russian Defence Minister Andrey Belousov in attendance, Kim described them as "heroes" who had chosen to sacrifice themselves in battle 
While North Korea has never officially acknowledged the death toll from the Kursk operation, a BBC Korea analysis of the memorial site estimated that 2,300 soldiers were killed fighting for Russia. 
Ukraine's intelligence arm, HUR, puts the figure at 3,000 killed and 1,500 injured. 
But aside from the combat experience, why did North Korea sacrifice so many of its best troops in a foreign war? 
An economic windfall 
The deployment has been a much-needed economic windfall for the country and a geopolitical win, according to Lim Soo-ho, a senior research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy, in Seoul. 
He estimates that arms sales to Russia and the troop deployment have netted the impoverished country close to $10bn. 
"North Korea's annual GDP is estimated at around $30bn (£22bn)," he told me. "That means they earned a third of a year's GDP over two and a half years through weapons exports and troop deployment, which, for an economy as small as North Korea's, is a very significant effect." 
In exchange for its manpower, North Korea gets food, oil and hard currency. While China says it complies with sanctions against Pyongyang, Russia does not. 
But equally important, the cooperation with Russia has shifted North Korea's long-term dependency on China. 
So in Beijing in September last year, Kim Jong Un was able to stand shoulder to shoulder with China's leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in the first public meeting of all three. Not quite as an equal, but no longer reliant on China alone. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
In September last year, Kim Jong Un stood alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the first public meeting of all three leaders 
This is significant, said Lim, "It's a major geopolitical shift". 
"Whenever things got difficult under isolation, North Korea would reach out first toward South Korea, Japan, or especially the US to try to normalise relations, that was the pattern of Korean Peninsula diplomacy. But now that ties with Russia have tightened, Kim Jong Un argues that the world is in a new Cold War, a multipolar system." 
The arrangement with Russia, which began as economic and military expediency appears to be developing into something deeper and longer-term. At this year's 9th Party Congress of the Korean Workers' Party, Kim Jong Un was emboldened and spoke of accomplishments that his grandfather Kim Il Sung and father Kim Jong Il never achieved. 
But dangers lie ahead. To date, no North Koreans have fought on Ukrainian or Russian-occupied Ukrainian land. If they did so, there would be diplomatic consequences, not least in South Korea, an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which so far has only provided "non-lethal" aid. 
This is something that President Zelensky has emphasised as he presses for Seoul to provide advanced military hardware, including air defence systems. He said that since June, preparations have been underway in Russia's Voronezh region to receive fresh North Korean forces and claimed that Pyongyang was preparing to transfer additional ballistic weapons to Russia. 
"Russia is helping North Korea learn modern warfare, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience. This poses a threat to every country in Asia that lies within range of North Korean missiles," he said in a presidential address in July. 
Only two North Korean soldiers were captured alive in battles with Ukrainian forces. That's a staggeringly low number, given that between 11,000 and 14,000 fought in the Kursk campaign. (Another was captured alive but died from combat-related injuries, according to the South Korean National Intelligence Service). 
Image source, @ZELENSKYYUA/X Image caption, 
Only two North Korean soldiers have been captured alive by Ukrainian forces 
Like their comrades who choose suicide over capture, neither man intended to be taken alive. 
"For Joseon (North Korean) soldiers, becoming a prisoner of war itself is a crime. That just isn't an option. We can't become POWs," one of the captured men told a South Korean MBC documentary crew who interviewed him in prison in Ukraine. 
Baek Pyeong-gang, not his real name, lay wounded from a drone strike for four days before being captured. He was tricked into surrendering when he mistook Ukrainian soldiers for his Russian allies. 
The second prisoner, Lee Kang-eun, also a pseudonym, told the journalist Kim Young-mi that he felt guilty he was still alive. Barely conscious, he was found by Ukrainian soldiers on the battlefield with extensive injuries to the arm and jaw. 
"I had no grenade or knives on me to self-blast (end my life)," he explained. 
He described scores of his colleagues killed by drones, early in the war. The battlefield "reeked of the smell of blood", he said. 
Neither man wants to return to North Korea, Lee said he believed that his family members would be "wiped out" as punishment for his capture. Both have said they want to be sent to South Korea, and Seoul is willing to take them. 
Image source, @ZELENSKYYUA/X Image caption, 
One of the North Korean soldiers captured alive said he did not want to return home, believing his family would be "wiped out" as punishment for his capture 
Only Russia, not Pyongyang, has asked for their return. 
But Ukraine, still intent on pressuring Seoul for military aid, has not committed to handing them over to South Korean authorities. Kyiv has said it will honour international human rights obligations which prevent the forced repatriation of prisoners of war. 
Their fate remains undecided, but what appears certain is that more North Koreans will join Russia's war. Their service has enormous economic and political value to Pyongyang; but Russia desperately needs them too. 
Four and a half years into Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it is facing a desperate manpower shortage. Western and Ukrainian intelligence agencies estimate that it is losing some 6,000 more troops a month than it can recruit. So, Moscow has been forced to turn to foreign fighters, from Colombia, Kenya, Cameroon and North Korea, to sustain its ranks. 
For Russia and North Korea, it is a mutually beneficial relationship, a coalition at a price. Ultimately, North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so.

articles.title: The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'
articles.summary: A new report warns Himalayan glaciers are melting faster, threatening India’s water, economy and communities.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Nur Photo via Getty Images Image caption, 
India's government says 56 glacial lakes had been classified as "very high risk" By Soutik Biswas 
India correspondent 
- Published 13 September 2026 
The Himalayas are approaching a dangerous threshold as glaciers melt faster, glacial lakes grow more unstable and the mountains face a widening gap in monitoring, according to new research. 
The findings come in the aftermath of devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, which killed more than 1,300 people and caused widespread destruction, highlighting the growing risks from a rapidly changing Himalayan environment. 
Himalayan glaciers are now losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, the report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with the Integrated Mountain Initiative and with technical contributions from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, says. 
Yet only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalaya-Karakoram region are being monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, according to the report. 
That monitoring gap matters because the physical landscape is changing rapidly. 
As glaciers retreat, they can leave behind expanding lakes held back by unstable deposits of rock and ice. At the same time, warming is destabilising permafrost - permanently frozen ground that can thaw as temperatures rise - and high mountain slopes, increasing the possibility of cascading hazards, the report says. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
A glacial lake outburst in 2023 triggered a flash flood, causing extensive damage in Sikkim 
India already has evidence of the scale of the risk. 
Some 18% of Indian land is Himalayan, yet the region accounts for about 35% of disasters, according to the report. 
The government told parliament in July that 56 glacial lakes had been classified as "very high risk" , external following a 2025 scientific assessment of 189 high-risk lakes in the Indian Himalayan region. The Central Water Commission is monitoring 2,485 glacial lakes larger than 10 hectares across India's Himalayan river basins, the government said. 
The Himalayas have already seen devastating examples of what can happen when glacial lakes burst their natural dams. 
In 2023, a glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim killed at least 70 people and caused widespread damage to roads, bridges and hydropower projects. In 2021, a similar disaster in Uttarakhand killed more than 200 people after a massive flood swept through the Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys. 
But the danger is not confined to spectacular floods. 
The Himalayas are a vast natural water system feeding rivers that sustain hundreds of millions of people across South Asia. ICIMOD says "peak water" , external is expected around mid-century in most Hindu Kush Himalayan river basins - the point at which glacier runoff reaches its maximum before declining as glaciers lose mass. 
The new research puts an unusually large economic number on that dependency. 
It estimates that Himalayan water underpins roughly 20% of India's GDP, sustaining wheat, rice, tea, hydropower and pilgrimage economies. Yet the mountain states capture only about 5% of that value, it says. 
"The Himalayas are the Third Pole," said economist Lord Nicholas Stern, chair of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics. "Unlike the Arctic or Antarctic, this pole has hundreds of millions of people living beneath it." 
Image source, Corbis via Getty Images Image caption, 
The Indian Himalayan region receives roughly 400 million visits a year 
"This is national and international infrastructure," he said, warning that the ecological system underpinning it is "approaching a tipping point". 
Not all the forces driving glacier loss are beyond the region's control. 
The Systemiq research estimates that roughly a third of Himalayan glacier melt is driven by black carbon, much of it originating from brick kilns in the plains. Soot deposited on snow and ice absorbs more sunlight and accelerates melting. 
Unlike global greenhouse-gas emissions, black-carbon pollution is a lever that India and its neighbours can act on directly, the report argues. 
"The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point, with millions of lives and livelihoods hanging in the balance," said Arushi Chopra, Systemiq's senior director and lead author. "Glaciers are melting faster than they were a decade ago." 
The report proposes 10 priority transitions, ranging from reducing black-carbon emissions and expanding glacier monitoring to improving disaster early-warning systems and changing the way tourism is developed in the mountains. 
One priority is to strengthen disaster preparedness, with governments agreeing in advance what action to take when hazards emerge - from evacuation to protecting vulnerable infrastructure. 
Another is to rethink tourism. The Indian Himalayan region receives roughly 400 million tourist visits a year, according to the report, and researchers argue that the objective should shift from maximising visitor numbers towards generating value that is retained and reinvested locally. 
Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD, said the risks were becoming increasingly complex. 
"Glaciers are retreating, permafrost and high-mountain slopes are becoming increasingly unstable, and communities and infrastructure downstream face growing risks from complex and cascading hazards," he said. 
And those risks do not stop at the borders drawn across the Himalayas. Such hazards, Gyamtsho said, "do not respect national borders, and no single country can address them alone". 
That makes cross-border monitoring, shared risk information and early-warning systems, and joint investment in resilience increasingly urgent - not just to save lives, but to protect the livelihoods and economies of hundreds of millions of people who depend on the mountains.

articles.title: Iran war reshapes Brics ties but also exposes divisions
articles.summary: Brics members agree they need a new global order but it's harder to answer what should replace it and how to get there.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
(From left) Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping pose for a photo at the Brics summit in Delhi By Azadeh Moshiri South Asia Correspondent ,  Reporting from Delhi 
- Published 13 September 2026 
This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table. 
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that together, the leaders next to him should increasingly become "rule-shapers", not "rule-takers". 
Among those listening were members of the Brics group, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. 
These are hardly natural allies. They have histories of border disputes and even military confrontations. 
India and China engaged in a deadly clash along their disputed border in 2020. Iran and the UAE have been on opposing ends of the war in the Middle East, with Tehran launching missiles and drones at its fellow Brics member as the conflict sent shockwaves across global economies. 
The fact that India was able to gather these leaders together in person is a feat in and of itself and testament to its diplomatic reach. The weekend also provided a platform for countries to reassess their relationships in light of the Iran war. 
But agreeing on what a new global order should look like and achieving clear, tangible outcomes was a much harder task, and that tension ran through this weekend's summit. 
A counterweight to Western influence 
For members such as China, Russia and Iran, Brics offers a vehicle to dilute the influence of the US and western Europe. 
But India has been reluctant to cast Brics as an anti-Western bloc. Modi himself said at the summit that the group is "not against anyone". 
That distinction matters for Delhi, which wants to preserve its relationships with nations at odds with each other. 
"There are countries in the grouping which would like it to become anti-western, but it is not that," says Anil Trigunayat, a veteran Indian diplomat and former ambassador. What India has achieved, in his view, is a push for "strategic autonomy in an era of war" and initiatives to "enhance greater collaboration amongst themselves". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Several Brics members would have been loath to draw US President Donald Trump's anger 
Inside the joint declaration 
The summit succeeded in delivering a joint declaration when divisions among members have rarely been so glaring. 
Twice earlier this year, meetings between Brics ministers had failed to produce a joint statement. This time a consensus was reached, but by side-stepping issues that members sharply disagree on, with few solutions. 
The "New Delhi Declaration" was adopted on the first day of the summit. But what is striking is what it doesn't say. 
On the war in the Middle East, the declaration urges "maximum restraint". It also condemns "attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities" but assigns no blame. 
It reiterates support for a two-state solution, opposes forced displacement of Palestinians or actions that could "legitimise or prolong occupation", framing it carefully around existing UN resolutions. 
It makes no mention at all of Russia's war in Ukraine, a departure from previous Brics declarations. 
There is similar caution on trade. It lists concerns over "indiscriminate rising tariffs" and condemns unilateral sanctions but stops short of naming the US, and is likely to avoid Washington's ire. 
- 
Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi 
Several Brics members would have been loath to draw President Donald Trump's anger, as he has previously called the group's proposals, including potentially linking central-bank digital currencies for cross-border trade, "anti-American". 
"Not mentioning any country by name, even as they condemned the conflict in the Middle East, bears the hallmark of India," says Praveen Donthi, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group. 
"I was pleasantly surprised that there was a strong reference to tariffs, because India could have wanted to be less direct about it, but perhaps this was a chance to convey their displeasure," he added. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian (right) and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan held talks at the sidelines of the Brics summit 
Beyond the summit 
In the wake of Trump's trade threats and the shock of the war in the Middle East, reshaping the global order has become a vital need for many member economies. 
What the summit did provide is a platform for meetings that seemed hard to imagine just a few months ago. 
Iran's Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince sat down for talks together - the highest-level face-to-face meeting known between the two countries since the war began. 
This weekend offered Tehran a chance to show that it does not stand alone amid the US and Israel's military attacks and economic pressure. 
As Iran tries to withstand US sanctions, Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" and a naval blockade on its ports, Pezeshkian pressed for deeper economic ties with Brics members, including Malaysia, India and Ethiopia. 
As for China, this was President Xi's first visit to Delhi in seven years. There has been deep mistrust between China and India since the 2020 border dispute, but those tensions have eased. There is also a large trade imbalance, with a deficit tilting heavily in China's favour. 
There was a cordial handshake between Xi and Modi, not the latter's signature hug. Xi also stayed for less than 24 hours, skipping the gala dinner hosted by Modi on Saturday night. 
But the weekend was still a big moment for two countries with such a difficult relationship. According to official readouts, the two leaders agreed to strengthen business ties and transport links and address barriers to trade. 
Trigunayat believes this is part of a gradual warming of relations in recent years, and that there is a will on both sides to work together. But whether it will produce substantial progress remains to be seen. 
"I always say we have to trust, but verify first," he says. 
What comes next? 
The summit showed that Brics can create space for rivals to talk and manoeuvre outside Western-dominated institutions. 
The harder question is what happens next. It's clear that members agree they need a new global order more than ever, but what exactly should replace it and how to get there is far more challenging to answer.

articles.title: Snapchat 'willing to implement' daily time limits for teens, boss tells BBC
articles.summary: Evan Speigel says it would be "an important step forward for the industry" in an interview with the BBC.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: CEO Evan Spiegel tells the BBC he would consider a time limit on Snapchat By Lily Jamali North America Technology correspondent 
- Published 18 minutes ago 
The boss of Snapchat says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action. 
Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that he believed setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry. " 
His comments came as the firm revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices. 
Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states. 
Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users. 
It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures. 
"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms." 
As part of Meta's August settlement , the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit . It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period. 
Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well. 
Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales. 
When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement." 
But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action. 
"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today." 
He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat. 
"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added. 
YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. 
Snap's smart glasses 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Evan Spiegel wearing the glasses at an event in June 
Spiegel was talking to the BBC as Snapchat's parent Snap Inc announced new features for its upcoming Specs glasses. 
He said the smart eyewear would use AI to suggest things for people to do based on what the tech learns about their goals, relationships and routines. 
"Rather than the way that people use chatbots today where you constantly have to ask for stuff, Specs can understand what's important to you, and then offer recommendations or offer next steps," he said. 
Like other smart glasses, Specs will use AI to let people see digital elements overlaid onto the world. 
But the tech won't come cheap - retailing at $2,195 in the US and £1,995 in the UK. 
"The target audience right now is early adopters of tech and developers as well as enterprise," Spiegel said. 
Image source, Snap Image caption, 
The firm wants people to use the glasses for various tasks, such as streaming video, and says it can offer live translation across 60 languages. 
With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses. 
"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel. 
"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world." 
Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars. 
The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market. 
Some online derisively call them " pervert glasses " over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach , while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet. 
Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta. 
Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people. 
A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo. 
The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening. 
Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device. 
Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

articles.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
articles.summary: A wrecked air force plane and destroyed buildings are among the images obtained by the BBC's partner CBS News.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Leaked photos reveal extensive damage at US bases in Gulf By Kayla Epstein and Bernd Debusmann Jr 
- Published 16 September 2026 
Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS. 
The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings. 
The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. 
One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public. 
"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face." 
The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran. 
One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal. 
Image source, CBS News Image caption, 
An undated photo of a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan air base in Saudi Arabia, about 62 miles (100km) south-east of the capital Riyadh 
While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo , apparently of the same radar aircraft in March. 
The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats. 
At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base. 
A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site. 
Image source, CBS News Image caption, 
Trailers destroyed by Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, Kuwait 
Image source, CBS News Image caption, 
Undated photo shows smoke billowing from a structure that sustained damage in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, Kuwait 
Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait. 
Damage to the site was reported in March , including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack. 
Brian Katulis, a former national security official under both Democratic and Republican administrations, said that the damage visible in the images showed that "America had not adequately prepared its defences". 
"And there is strong evidence that US adversaries like China and Russia may have helped Iran in targeting," added Katulis, now a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. "The Trump administration has done nothing to address these vulnerabilities." 
Image source, CBS News Image caption, 
Damage to a building can be seen in this photo from Camp Arifjan, Kuwait 
The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict". 
It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said. 
In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues. 
The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions". 
A separate report , external from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7. 
The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b). 
CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports. 
Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report. 
Brian Katulis of the Middle East Institute said that while "these costs show how the Trump administration burned through precious military resources without having much to show for it", the greater damage had been to broader US military readiness. 
"The United States had to divert military assets from Asia to the Middle East, leaving America and its partners in Asia more exposed and vulnerable to China," he said. 
"In addition, the depletion of US munitions makes Russia more willing to probe vulnerabilities with America's NATO allies and continue its aggressive war against Ukraine." 
While the US has the financial resources to address the equipment losses, it is already facing budgetary problems and may not be able to do so fast enough to prepare for potential flare-ups in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, he added. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: What does the munitions shortage mean for the US? 
Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country. 
Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel. 
On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval. 
The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matte r ahead of the US midterm elections in November. 
It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter. 
The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US. 
The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job".

articles.title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
articles.summary: The US president has pushed the issue to the forefront of American politics - even at the risk of losing supporters.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI? By Anthony Zurcher 
North America correspondent 
- Published 16 September 2026 
According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax. 
It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term. 
Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology. 
The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party. 
- 
OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms 
- Published 14 hours ago 
- 
AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act 
- Published 1 day ago 
- 
Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards 
- Published 1 day ago 
None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will. 
Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies. 
"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate." 
Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI. 
"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing." 
Figure caption, 
Watch: "Great" or "alarming" - Should AI be reined in? 
According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement. 
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies." 
A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order. 
It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs. 
Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development. 
But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead? 
The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI 
Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years. 
According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026. 
The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI. 
Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion. 
Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind. 
"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins." 
The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control. 
Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative. 
Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump 
Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president. 
"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear." 
Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration. 
These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump. 
In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development. 
"This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to." 
Figure caption, 
Watch: AI needs a 'brake pedal', Anthropic co-founder tells BBC 
Where the political debate goes from here is an open question. 
With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric. 
With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances. 
But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president. 
Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming. 
"It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.

articles.title: Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump
articles.summary: The Canadian PM is in Strasbourg this week seeking a "unique alliance" - and there is one clear catalyst.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Carney is a guest of von der Leyen in Strasbourg this week By Katya Adler Europe editor 
- Published 16 September 2026 
"Wouldn't it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" asked Finland's President Alexander Stubb this summer. 
The question was rather tongue-in-cheek. US President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state - causing deep offence amongst many Canadians. 
Finland is one of the EU's 27 member states and a close ally of Canada as a fellow Arctic nation. Teasing tones aside, President Stubb put his finger squarely on the pulse of deepening EU-Canadian relations. "Canada is more Europe-minded than most Europeans!" is a smiling retort you often hear in Brussels at the moment. 
On Sunday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. 
And in a speech on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to work "on opening the door" for Canada to be the EU's "associate member" - which would involve closer ties on various sectors including manufacturing and energy. 
The catalyst for this very public, ardent new love-in is Donald Trump. Just the other day, the US president posted a map of North America on his Truth Social site, including Canada and Greenland - a territory that's part of EU country Denmark - all overlaid with the US flag. 
- 
Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump 
- Published 13 hours ago 
- 
Carney eyes 'unique alliance' with EU as trade war with US intensifies 
- Published 2 days ago 
- 
Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map 
- Published 8 September 
Trade negotiations between the US and Canada broke down late last month. European countries, which have been hit by their own Trump tariffs, have privately watched the spat play out with a mixture of interest and, for many, admiration. 
While the EU, led by the European Commission, simply accepted new blanket Trump tariffs without fighting back, Carney has prominently stood up to the US president, swiftly imposing counter-tariffs on the United States. 
When it comes to courting the EU, Canada appears to some to be even keener than one of the bloc's closest neighbours. 
"Canada right now seems more interested than the UK to get as close to Brussels as possible, as a non member state" says Mark Leonard, director of the European Council of Foreign Relations think tank. "It's remarkable." 
Canada, but not the UK, successfully joined the European Union's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence fund earlier this year. The UK remained on the sidelines following a row over costs and political tensions. A summit designed to reset and improve EU-UK relations has just been delayed - again - over cross-Channel differences. 
By contrast this week, Carney is invited as a special guest to the European Commission President's annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France on Wednesday. Carney will hold a speech in the European Parliament there on Thursday, a day after President von der Leyen outlines the EU's political and policy priorities. 
Officials on both sides insist this is more than just "blah blah politics", as one EU diplomat put it to me. He was speaking on condition of anonymity so as to be able to discuss the subject freely. Carney and von der Leyen are both expected to mention plans to forge closer ties. "As close as you can get without (Canada) actually becoming an EU member," the diplomat told me. 
'Trump effect' prompts efforts to diversify - but are they achievable? 
The unofficial aim for both Brussels and Canada, I'm told, is to reduce reliance on Washington in several key areas: 
- 
Digital and tech developments, in which the US and China dominate 
- 
Energy: Canada is rich in liquified natural gas (LNG) the EU needs since it cut back its energy dependency on Russia 
- 
Raw materials and critical minerals: Canada has them in abundance 
- 
Trade and defence procurement: Canada has been on a "buy European" spree of late, purchasing German attack submarines, for example, and airborne early-warning planes from Sweden's Saab. Its view appears to be: why reward the US by buying American equipment after being slapped with trade tariffs amounting to 50% in some sectors? 
A Nanos opinion poll from April suggests more than four in five Canadians favour strengthening ties with the EU. 
Close to three in five support Canada actually joining the bloc, though Article 49 of the EU Constitution would appear to make that impossible. Without wanting to seem facetious, the European Union is not (yet) the Eurovision Song Contest, in which indisputably non-European Israel and Australia have - controversially - been allowed to compete. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: How much can Canada fight back in its trade war with the US? 
Back to trade: ties between Canada and the EU are far from novel. The EU is already Canada's second-largest trading partner - albeit far behind the US, which buys about 70% of Canadian exports. 
The far-reaching Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) trade deal was agreed just under a decade ago and has been provisionally implemented, eliminating 99% of tariffs on Canadian goods exports. 
Privately, European officials admit this renewed high-level courtship between Ottawa and Brussels has everything to do with the actions of Trump's second term in office. 
Image source, Getty Images 
The US president is by now infamous amongst US allies for what they view as his unpredictability and his penchant to use trade or security ties as leverage. 
There's a growing sense in Europe - which has, since World War Two, looked to the US as its closest ally abroad - and in Canada, whose economy has been intertwined with the US for decades, that neither can any longer fully rely on Washington. They believe it's time to diversify. 
"The Canadian government is committed to trade diversification, doubling non-US trades in the next 10 years, and doing more with the European Union will be very key to achieving that target," Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association (CEUTIA) told the BBC. 
An even tighter Canadian-EU alliance, covering far more sectors than trade alone, would continue a recent trend of both parties to form new association agreements around the world. In Canada's case, this includes a sectoral deal with China, which raised international eyebrows earlier this year. 
EU insiders put all of this down to the "Trump effect". 
- 
Carney gambles on the world's biggest investors betting on Canada 
- Published 2 days ago 
- 
The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts 
- Published 31 August 
- 
What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans 
- Published 9 September 
But decoupling from the US altogether would seem unrealistic - for both Canada and the EU. 
The US is the EU's largest overall trading partner, if you take goods and services together. 
Canada and the US have the largest bilateral trading relationship in the world, valued at nearly US$900bn (£668bn) last year. This dwarfs the $130bn of total EU-Canada bilateral trade during the same timeframe. 
The vast majority of Canadian exports head to the US. 
So, Ottawa could sign new trade agreements, but replacing customers and supply chains built around America's massive market would be a tall order. 
This week, I hear, Carney and von der Leyen will vociferously defend a global system of rules-based trade. 
"This is not about trying to keep the past alive. We need to forge a new rules-based future in trade and beyond. With or without Washington," diplomats tell me. 
There's an EU-Canada summit scheduled for the end of next month. After that, working groups are expected to start the less-than-sexy task of tackling the legal and technical details in the different areas in which the EU and Canada now hope to establish closer ties. 
So are EU and Canada really becoming BFFs? 
A huge turning point for Europe in its attitude towards Washington came early this year when Trump refused to rule out taking Greenland from fellow Nato power, Denmark, by force. 
Around that time, Carney - who's also the former governor of the Bank of England - gave a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, calling on middle-sized countries to stick together against economic coercion by global super-powers. Europe sat up and took notice. 
Why then, you might ask, haven't Europe's leaders been more outspoken in their support for the Canadian prime minister during the current escalation in trade tensions with the US? Carney has been defiant, declaring that Canada was "at war" with the US over trade. 
He swiftly imposed counter-tariffs on the US in the name of "sovereignty". 
Paolo Gentiloni, a former EU economy commissioner and former Italian premier, commented on social media: "Here is a speech I would like to hear in Europe." 
Figure caption, 
Watch: "Absolutely ridiculous": Canadians react to new tariff tensions with the US 
Yet - in public - Europe's leaders have remained cautiously quiet. 
Though not, it seems, out of any lack of support for Mark Carney. 
A number of Europe's leaders, like Finland's president - but also French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, herself once a true Trump fan - are involved in behind-the-scene chats with Carney about deepening relations, I'm told. 
But - and it's a big but - no leading European politician wants to stick his or her neck out for Carney in public right now and risk having voters at home blame them for possibly incurring the wrath of - and fresh punitive tariffs from - the US president. 
Over the coming months, every large country in the EU holds key elections. Germany's took place just over a week ago. France chooses a new president in April and early May. Italy, Spain and Poland have yet to set a date for their parliamentary elections. 
When it comes to applauding Carney right now, Europe's leaders are hiding behind the EU institutions. 
Under EU rules, the European Commission deals with trade on behalf of the member states. The EU Commission and EU parliament presidents invited Carney to Strasbourg this week. 
But some officials I speak to in Brussels warn that Carney should also wake up and smell the European coffee. 
Brussels may feel warmly towards Canada, and believe Ottawa shares many of the same values and priorities, but there are still loud EU voices, like France, that prefer to prevent non-member countries from getting too favourable a deal. 
That's despite pressure on the EU to show more flexibility when it comes to accommodating allies, considering the turbulent times we live in. 
It's a conundrum the UK faces too. 
Carney flies to Liverpool later this week, after leaving the European Parliament, for his first face-to-face meeting with new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham. 
As well as discussing UK-Canada ties, who knows - might the two men end up debating ways to best woo the EU, too?

articles.title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
articles.summary: The announcement by the US points to a developing field of modern warfare in the Earth's orbit.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Could there be an arms race in space? The BBC's defence correspondent explains what the US announcement means By Robert Greenall 
- Published 15 September 2026 
The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena. 
Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit. 
So what could this weapon be, and what is the wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry? 
Space has been a militarised domain since the start of the space age - in the late 1960s, the Soviet Union deployed weapons up there. The Istrebitel Sputnikov (IS; Satellite Destroyer) programme was made up of satellites that were designed to release projectiles that detonated, releasing shrapnel into the path of another (usually American) satellite. 
Nowadays, advanced militaries deploy satellites in space for a range of purposes, including reconnaissance, secure communications, detecting missile launches and providing precise location information for targeted strikes. 
As warfare becomes more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Some types of space weaponry could create a lot of debris and destruction 
Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US. 
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. 
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless." 
Bowen also would not rule out a riskier and more disruptive type of weaponry, which could create debris and destruction. 
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said. 
A type of "close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well." 
As to whether rivals such as Russia and China have similar weaponry already in orbit, is difficult to tell. 
"If we're looking towards China and Russia, they have both displayed activity," Juliana Suess, a former research fellow at RUSI and researcher at the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (German Institute for International and Security Affairs), told the BBC. 
"For example, with Russia, we've seen some activity that hints at being a co-orbital weapons test. So we saw something that might indicate that they shot a projectile as a test in orbit. 
"There are others out there, but without knowing the details, what the American [weapon] is, it's difficult to draw comparisons." 
-

- Published 21 May 2025 
- 
Satellite killers: What a war in space might look like 
But while the weapon placed in orbit may be unusual, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time. 
In a later BBC interview, Bowen was dismissive of China's reaction to the US announcement which warned against an arms race in space, describing it as "the pot calling the kettle black". 
"If you're already an expert... you know how hollow those words are coming from the Russian and Chinese governments," he said. 
"The United States, Russia and China and also India have all developed different kinds of anti-satellite or counter-space weapons, and Russia and China have put a lot of technologies in space which have a lot of weapons potential," he added. 
In fact in the past 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites. 
"Theoretically, these RPO [satellites]can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC. 
Bowen added that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit." 
This, he said, could be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites. 
However, some types of space weaponry also have the potential to create huge amounts of space junk. 
Dr Mark Hilborne, a specialist in space security and weaponisation at King's College, said direct ascent anti-satellite missile tests, such as one carried out by China in 2007, leave a great deal of debris in orbit for a very long time. 
Suess said debris from that test was still in orbit and still dangerous. 
"It doesn't have to be a sort of huge piece of metal to do any damage, it can be a tiny piece of plastic, given the velocity that we're talking about in orbit," she said. 
The nuclear threat 
Thornton said that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability. 
"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike [satellites] in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT [air-launched antisatellite] missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he said. 
"From the Russian point of view, they see Nato as having much better and more satellites than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat." 
Thornton added a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EMP [nuclear electromagnetic pulse] blast would 'fry' any unhardened satellite over a wide expanse." 
So what is the likelihood of a nuclear conflict in space? Only if it was happening on the ground as well. 
"What could happen in space is not something that would happen in isolation, really," Bowen said. "Nothing could happen, or something could." 
Figure caption, 
Watch: US Space Force Guardians spring into action during training exercise 
Given that weapons for use in space have been around for so long, why did the US announcement come when it did? Experts agree that it's not a major development as such, more a political signal. 
Bowen suggested that it could be a response to Chinese developments. 
"China has modernised its military forces over the past 30 years," he said. "It has put a lot more military satellites in space and has presented a lot more targets that are worth the American military going after and hitting." 
"There's much more incentive for American space weapons now because China has a lot of vulnerability to space in the same way that the Americans have." 
This situation seems to have created a curious imbalance. 
Thornton said that, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, because it has so few satellites, unlike China and the US. It would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring satellites designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers," he said.
